claim: The BB-QTL mapping approach allows construction, genotyping, and phenotyping of 100,000 offspring of a budding yeast cross.
source: Here, we introduce barcoded bulk quantitative trait locus (BB-QTL) mapping, which allows us to construct, genotype, and phenotype 100,000 offspring of a budding yeast cross, two orders of magnitude larger than the previous state of the art.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the scale of the BB-QTL approach and compares it to previous methods.

claim: BB-QTL mapping is two orders of magnitude larger than the previous state of the art in yeast QTL studies.
source: Here, we introduce barcoded bulk quantitative trait locus (BB-QTL) mapping, which allows us to construct, genotype, and phenotype 100,000 offspring of a budding yeast cross, two orders of magnitude larger than the previous state of the art.
evidence: The abstract provides a direct comparison to previous QTL mapping studies in terms of sample size.

claim: The genetic architecture of eighteen complex traits involves hundreds of small-effect loci densely spaced throughout the genome.
source: We use this panel to map the genetic basis of eighteen complex traits, finding that the genetic architecture of these traits involves hundreds of small-effect loci densely spaced throughout the genome, many with widespread pleiotropic effects across multiple traits.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main finding about the polygenic nature of the traits studied.

claim: Many loci have widespread pleiotropic effects across multiple traits.
source: We use this panel to map the genetic basis of eighteen complex traits, finding that the genetic architecture of these traits involves hundreds of small-effect loci densely spaced throughout the genome, many with widespread pleiotropic effects across multiple traits.
evidence: The abstract states that many loci affect multiple traits.

claim: Epistasis plays a central role in the genetic architecture of complex traits, with thousands of interactions.
source: Epistasis plays a central role, with thousands of interactions that provide insight into genetic networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly mentions the role and scale of epistatic interactions.

claim: GWAS studies in humans now involve sample sizes of hundreds of thousands or even millions of individuals.
source: Studies investigating the genetic basis of important phenotypes such as height, BMI, and risk for diseases such as schizophrenia now involve sample sizes of hundreds of thousands or even millions of individuals.
evidence: The introduction describes the scale of modern GWAS studies.

claim: GWAS studies have shown that traits like height, BMI, and schizophrenia risk are very highly polygenic.
source: The corresponding increase in power has shown that these traits are very highly polygenic, with a large fraction of segregating polymorphisms (hundreds of thousands of loci) having a causal effect on phenotype (Yang et al., 2010; International Schizophrenia Consortium et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites studies showing the polygenic nature of these traits.

claim: The vast majority of loci identified in GWAS have extremely small effects.
source: However, the vast majority of these loci have extremely small effects, and we remain unable to explain most of the heritable variation in many of these traits (the 'missing heritability' problem; Manolio et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction discusses the small effect sizes of most GWAS loci and the missing heritability problem.

claim: QTL mapping studies in model organisms like budding yeast tend to have much smaller sample sizes of at most a few thousand individuals.
source: In contrast to GWAS, quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies in model organisms such as budding yeast tend to have much smaller sample sizes of at most a few thousand individuals (Steinmetz et al., 2002; Bloom et al., 2013; Burga et al., 2019; Mackay and Huang, 2018; Bergelson and Roux, 2010).
evidence: The introduction contrasts QTL mapping sample sizes with GWAS.

claim: Most QTL mapping studies are only able to identify relatively few loci (typically at most dozens) with a causal effect on phenotype.
source: Due to their lower power, most of these studies are only able to identify relatively few loci (typically at most dozens, though see below) with a causal effect on phenotype.
evidence: The introduction describes the typical number of QTL detected in previous studies.

claim: Despite identifying few loci, QTL mapping studies explain most or all of the observed phenotypic variation in many traits studied.
source: Despite this, these few loci explain most or all of the observed phenotypic variation in many of the traits studied (Fay, 2013).
evidence: The introduction notes the apparent success of QTL mapping in explaining heritability despite detecting few loci.

claim: GWAS studies suffer from statistical confounders due to population structure.
source: For example, GWAS studies suffer from statistical confounders due to population structure, and the low median minor allele frequencies in these studies limit power and mapping resolution (Bloom et al., 2013; Sohail et al., 2019; King et al., 2012; Consortium, 2012).
evidence: The introduction discusses technical limitations of GWAS.

claim: Low median minor allele frequencies in GWAS studies limit power and mapping resolution.
source: For example, GWAS studies suffer from statistical confounders due to population structure, and the low median minor allele frequencies in these studies limit power and mapping resolution (Bloom et al., 2013; Sohail et al., 2019; King et al., 2012; Consortium, 2012).
evidence: The introduction discusses technical limitations of GWAS.

claim: The limited power of existing QTL mapping studies may cause them to aggregate numerous linked small-effect causal loci into single large-effect 'composite' QTL.
source: Alternatively, the limited power of existing QTL mapping studies in model organisms such as budding yeast (perhaps combined with the relatively high functional density of these genomes) may cause them to aggregate numerous linked small-effect causal loci into single large-effect 'composite' QTL.
evidence: The introduction proposes a hypothesis about how limited power affects QTL detection.

claim: Advanced crosses improve fine-mapping resolution by introducing more recombination breakpoints.
source: One direction has been to use advanced crosses to introduce more recombination breakpoints into mapping panels (She and Jarosz, 2018). This improves fine-mapping resolution and under some circumstances may be able to resolve composite QTL into individual causal loci, but it does not in itself improve power to detect small-effect alleles.
evidence: The introduction discusses how advanced crosses improve mapping resolution but not power.

claim: Advanced crosses do not in themselves improve power to detect small-effect alleles.
source: This improves fine-mapping resolution and under some circumstances may be able to resolve composite QTL into individual causal loci, but it does not in itself improve power to detect small-effect alleles.
evidence: The introduction discusses limitations of advanced crosses.

claim: Multiparental crosses reduce the allele frequency of each variant.
source: However, because multiparental crosses reduce the allele frequency of each variant (and in round-robin schemes each variant is present in only a few matings), these studies also have limited power to detect small-effect alleles.
evidence: The introduction discusses how multiparental crosses affect allele frequencies and power.

claim: In round-robin mating schemes, each variant is present in only a few matings.
source: However, because multiparental crosses reduce the allele frequency of each variant (and in round-robin schemes each variant is present in only a few matings), these studies also have limited power to detect small-effect alleles.
evidence: The introduction describes a characteristic of round-robin mating schemes.

claim: The ability to identify small-effect alleles in large diploid panels scales only with the number of unique haploid parents rather than the number of diploid genotypes.
source: However, the ability to identify small-effect alleles scales only with the number of unique haploid parents rather than the number of diploid genotypes, so these studies also lack power for this purpose.
evidence: The introduction explains why large diploid panels have limited power for detecting small-effect alleles.

claim: The BB-QTL approach uses unique DNA barcoding of every strain to conduct sequencing-based bulk phenotype measurements.
source: We combined several recent technical advances to overcome the challenges of QTL mapping at the scale of 100,000 segregants: (i) unique DNA barcoding of every strain, which allows us to conduct sequencing-based bulk phenotype measurements
evidence: The introduction describes the technical approach used in BB-QTL mapping.

claim: The BB-QTL approach uses a highly multiplexed sequencing approach that exploits knowledge of parental genotypes to accurately infer segregant genotypes from low-coverage (<1x) sequence data.
source: (ii) a highly multiplexed sequencing approach that exploits our knowledge of the parental genotypes to accurately infer the genotype of each segregant from low-coverage (<1x) sequence data
evidence: The introduction describes the genotyping approach used in BB-QTL mapping.

claim: The BB-QTL approach uses liquid handling robotics and combinatorial pooling to create, array, manipulate, and store the segregant collection in 96/384-well plates.
source: (iii) liquid handling robotics and combinatorial pooling to create, array, manipulate, and store this segregant collection in 96/384-well plates
evidence: The introduction describes the automation approach used in BB-QTL mapping.

claim: The BB-QTL approach uses a highly conservative cross-validated forward search approach to confidently infer large numbers of small-effect QTL.
source: (iv) a highly conservative cross-validated forward search approach to confidently infer large numbers of small-effect QTL.
evidence: The introduction describes the statistical approach used in BB-QTL mapping.

source: because we use an F1 rather than an advanced cross, we have a high density of SNPs relative to recombination breakpoints in each individual (>700 SNPs between recombination breakpoints on average).

source: We find that at 0.1 x coverage and above, our HMM approach confidently assigns genotypes at almost all loci (posterior probability of >92% of the inferred genotype at >99% of loci; see Appendix 1—figure 2 and Appendix 1 for a discussion of our validation of these posterior probability estimates).

claim: The genotyping is accurate, with detectable error only very near recombination breakpoints.
